questions.def: "Have to get something done" means arranging for someone to do it.
questions.question: I have to ___ my car repaired this week.

questions.def: "Gotten" is the American English past participle of "get".
questions.question: She has ___ a promotion at work recently.

questions.def: "Got" is the past simple form of "get", indicating a completed action.
questions.question: They ___ married last summer.

questions.def: "Have got" means "have received" in British English.
questions.question: Have you ___ the email I sent yesterday?

questions.def: "Little" means "almost no" and is used with uncountable nouns.
questions.question: I have ___ time to finish the project.

questions.def: "Have" expresses possession or a general feeling.
questions.question: I ___ a feeling that something is wrong.

questions.def: "Haven't been" is used to describe a state that started in the past.
questions.question: We haven't ___ in touch since we moved.

questions.def: "Some" is used in affirmative sentences to indicate quantity.
questions.question: He has ___ difficulty understanding the instructions.

questions.def: "Am getting used to" describes an ongoing adjustment.
questions.question: I ___ used to waking up early.

questions.def: "Have no idea" is a common idiom meaning "don't know".
questions.question: I have ___ idea what you're talking about.

questions.def: "Never" indicates a lack of experience.
questions.question: She has ___ been to Paris.

questions.def: "Have" indicates possession or a scheduled event.
questions.question: We ___ a meeting scheduled for tomorrow.

questions.def: "Have you not" indicates something unfinished at the present time.
questions.question: Have you ___ finished your homework yet?

questions.def: "Have had" is the present perfect tense of "have".
questions.question: They have ___ a good time at the party.

questions.def: "Got something done" means arranging for someone to do it.
questions.question: I ___ my hair cut yesterday.

questions.def: "Little" suggests almost no money remaining.
questions.question: He has ___ money left after paying the bills.

questions.def: "Rarely" means not very often.
questions.question: We have ___ seen such a beautiful sunset.

questions.def: "Have to" expresses obligation.
questions.question: They ___ to leave early.

questions.def: "Have got" means "have received" in British English.
questions.question: Have you ___ your driving license yet?

questions.def: "Some" is used in affirmative sentences to indicate quantity.
questions.question: I have ___ problems with my computer lately.

questions.def: "Got" is the past simple form of "get", indicating a completed action.
questions.question: I ___ a headache this morning.

questions.def: "Have no time" is a common idiom meaning "don't have time".
questions.question: We have ___ time to waste.

questions.def: "Already" indicates that something has happened before now.
questions.question: She has ___ visited Italy.

questions.def: "Have something done" means arranging for someone else to do it.
questions.question: I ___ my hair cut yesterday at the new salon.

questions.def: "Has got used to" means she is now accustomed to something.
questions.question: She ___ used to waking up early, but now she enjoys it.

questions.def: "Got" is the simple past tense, indicating a completed action.
questions.question: We ___ a promotion after all our hard work.

questions.def: "Had got" implies they obtained the tickets before our arrival.
questions.question: By the time we arrived, they ___ all the tickets.

questions.def: "Have got to" expresses obligation or necessity.
questions.question: They ___ to finish the project by Friday.

questions.def: "Have something done" means arranging for someone to do it.
questions.question: I ___ my apartment cleaned every month.

questions.def: "Get a chance" is the correct idiom for obtaining an opportunity.
questions.question: I didn't ___ a chance to speak with her yesterday.
